_meta.topic: Chartering and crew: private jet charter, hiring a pilot for an owned aircraft, crewed boat charter, and car hire with a driver

conventions.sourceType: 'primary' = the operator, authority, or statute itself publishes the figure; 'secondary' = a broker, guide, aggregator, or press item reporting it
conventions.confirmed: true = the figure was read on the cited page during this session; false = seen only in a search-engine summary or not verifiable on the page
conventions.currency: Each figure carries its own currency code. Operator price pages are advertising, not regulated tariffs, and change without notice.

notes: Jet-charter 'hourly rates' from brokers are ranges for the aircraft only. Brokers state they exclude some or all of: federal excise tax, segment fees, landing/handling/FBO fees, overnight crew costs, daily minimums, repositioning, de-icing and catering.
Almost no operator publishes a fixed price for a specific route; route prices below are brokers' published estimates.

BLS figures come from the BLS public API v2 (OEWS, May 2025 estimates, reported as year 2025). The bls.gov HTML pages refused automated access, so the page URL is the canonical citation and the API is the retrieval route.

NetJets does not publish charter or fractional rates on its own site. Third-party comparison sites (e.g., https://privatejetcardcomparisons.com/providers/netjets-marquis-jet/) report estimates such as an entry 1/16 share near $850,000, monthly management fees of $12,000-$28,000 and occupied-hour rates of $8,500-$18,500; these are unverified estimates, not published prices.

Both sites returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches. Search summaries attributed to them: turboprop about $2,000-$3,000/hr, light jet $2,600-$3,500/hr, midsize $3,500-$5,500/hr, heavy $8,000-$13,000/hr. Not confirmed on the page.

federalExciseTax.applicability: Applies to charter flights on aircraft operated for hire (Part 135 charter). A charter customer is billed the 7.5% on the charter price plus the segment fee per passenger per segment. Whether a given arrangement is 'commercial' for FET is a fact question; the IRS and NBAA discuss it at https://nbaa.org/flight-department-administration/tax-issues/federal-taxes/fet/.

dailyMinimumAndRepositioning.value: Charter operators commonly bill a daily minimum of 2.0 to 3.0 flight hours per aircraft per day, and bill repositioning (ferry) legs when the aircraft must fly empty to the pickup or back to base.

sources.note: Lists daily minimums as excluded from the hourly rate; describes repositioning

dailyMinimumAndRepositioning.note: The daily minimum is a commercial practice, not a regulation. No statute or FAA rule sets it.

privatePilot.publisher: Legal Information Institute (Cornell) reproducing the eCFR
privatePilot.rule: Except as provided in paragraphs (b) through (h), a holder of a private pilot certificate may not act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying passengers or property for compensation or hire, nor act as pilot in command for compensation or hire.
privatePilot.costSharing: 61.113(c): a private pilot may not pay less than the pro rata share of a flight's operating expenses with passengers, limited to fuel, oil, airport expenditures or rental fees.
privatePilot.exceptions: (b) flying incidental to a business or employment with no passengers or property carried for hire; (d) charitable, nonprofit or community-event flights under 91.146; (e) search-and-location reimbursement; (f) aircraft salesman demonstrations with at least 200 hours; (g) glider or unpowered ultralight towing; (h) light-sport production flight tests; (i) BasicMed conditions.
privatePilot.gameMeaning: An owner cannot pay a private pilot to fly the owner's plane. A paid pilot needs at least a commercial certificate.

commercialPilot.publisher: Legal Information Institute (Cornell) reproducing the eCFR
commercialPilot.rule: A commercial pilot may act as pilot in command of an aircraft carrying persons or property for compensation or hire, and may act as pilot in command for compensation or hire, when qualified under Part 61 and the applicable operating rules.
commercialPilot.note: Flying the owner's own aircraft for pay (the owner supplies the aircraft, the pilot is paid only to fly) is a Part 91 operation a commercial pilot may do. Supplying both aircraft and pilot to someone for pay is a Part 135 charter needing an air carrier certificate; that line is FAA policy (the 'holding out' and 'dry vs. wet lease' doctrine) not pinned to a number here.

canadaUkIrelandMexico.note: Not researched to the same standard. Equivalent rules exist (Transport Canada CARs 401; UK CAA and Ireland IAA under EASA Part-FCL, where a PPL holder may not be paid; Mexico AFAC) but no figures were retrieved.

passengerForHire.rule: A passenger for hire is one for whom consideration is contributed as a condition of carriage on the vessel, directly or indirectly, to anyone with an interest in the vessel.

uninspectedPassengerVessel.rule: A vessel under 100 gross tons carrying not more than 6 passengers, at least one for hire, or chartered with the crew provided or specified by the owner and carrying not more than 6 passengers. This is the 'six-pack' category.

smallPassengerVessel.rule: A vessel under 100 gross tons carrying more than 6 passengers with at least one for hire, or chartered with crew provided and carrying more than 6 passengers, or chartered with no crew provided and carrying more than 12 passengers. Such a vessel must be Coast Guard inspected and certificated.

captainLicense.rule: Each self-propelled uninspected passenger vessel must be under the direction and control of an individual holding a merchant mariner credential endorsed as Operator of Uninspected Passenger Vessels (OUPV, the 'six-pack' license) or higher.

bareboat.value: A true bareboat (demise) charter hands the charterer the vessel without crew; the charterer operates it or hires any captain they choose, and no Coast Guard license is needed to run it recreationally. If the owner supplies or dictates the captain, it is legally a crewed charter and the six-pack/inspected-vessel rules apply. A bareboat charter carrying more than 12 passengers is a small passenger vessel.

sources.publisher: U.S. Coast Guard Auxiliary, Passengers for Hire trifold

bareboat.stateRules: State boater-education cards still apply to a bareboat charterer at the helm (New York 'Brianna's Law' and California's Boater Card phase-in); not researched here.

gratuity.value: 15-20% is the customary US crew gratuity on a crewed charter; one NYC operator suggests 18-22%.

sources.note: Search summary: 15-20% industry standard, or no less than $200 total

outsideUS.note: London (Thames), Dublin, Toronto, Vancouver and Mexico City crewed day-charter rates were not retrieved. Rules differ: in the UK a commercially operated small vessel falls under the MCA Small Vessel Code; in Canada under the Canada Shipping Act 2001 (a pleasure craft 'chartered' with a captain becomes a commercial vessel).

regulator.value: TLC does not set passenger fares for black cars or limousines; the base sets them. TLC licenses the drivers and vehicles. Its minimum-pay rules cover drivers of High-Volume For-Hire Services (Uber, Lyft) and 'do not ... set the exact driver payment or passenger fare.'

hvfhsDriverMinimumPay.note: A 3.36% CPI-W increase applied 2026-03-01 (TLC Industry Notice 26-03). This is driver pay, not a passenger fare.

blsChauffeurWage.note: What a chauffeur earns, as opposed to what a customer pays per hour.

regulator.value: In California, charter-party carriers (limousines and hourly chauffeur service) are licensed by the California Public Utilities Commission (TCP permit); the CPUC does not set their hourly prices.

hourlyChauffeur.note: No single LA operator's rate page was read. Search summaries of LA operators showed executive sedans at about $70-$119/hr and SUVs at $95-$149/hr with 2-3 hour minimums and 15-20% gratuity suggested; not confirmed on a page.

NetJets publishes no prices; all NetJets figures in circulation are third-party estimates.
Alaska/Hawaii international facilities tax for 2026: IRS Form 720 instructions say $11.70, NATA's post says $11.30. Only the IRS figure should be used.
UK APD from 2027-04-01 (higher rate extended to jets over 5.7 tonnes; £146.63 / £1,132.76) was seen only in broker summaries.
King Air 350 contract day rate (PIC $1,500-$2,000) and CrewBlast per diem ($75-$150) are from search summaries, not read on the page.
Paramount Business Jets' own rates changed between an older indexed page (light jet $2,900-$3,500) and the page read (light jet $3,750-$4,200); brokers reprice often.
PrivateFly's hourly table (e.g., Citation XLS £2,684/hr) is well below US broker ranges for the same class; it may predate recent increases.
No operator publishes a fixed Teterboro-Van Nuys or New York-London price; all route figures are broker estimates.
Marina del Rey crewed-charter rates are from marketplace search summaries and one operator whose site failed to resolve; no Marina del Rey figure is confirmed on a page.
Los Angeles hourly chauffeur rates for a sedan/SUV service were not confirmed on an operator page; only a drive-your-own-car service (Jeevz) was.
Addison Lee does not publish hourly-hire prices; its one-hour minimum and 10-miles-per-hour cap were seen only in a search summary.
All City Chauffeurs (Dublin) page shows a 2022 copyright; prices may be stale.
BC limousine one-hour minimum time charge is from a search summary of the PTB rules, not the Rule 19 page.
Regulator statements for London (TfL), Dublin (NTA), Toronto (Chapter 546) and California (CPUC) are background knowledge not verified on 2026-09-30.
Crewed boat charter figures for London, Dublin, Toronto, Vancouver and Mexico City, and pilot-hire figures outside the US, were not retrieved.
No published day rate for a contract pilot on a single-engine piston other than Cirrus instructor/mentor rates was found.
